title: OpenAI says teen ChatGPT use limited but research finds it an 'unacceptable risk'
content:
OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens was designed to promote healthier use of the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot, but new research has found its important safety features fall short.
The major AI firm rolled out many teen safety guardrails in August, including curbs on emotional dependence and new parental alerts for problematic use.
On Wednesday, OpenAI said it found average teen use of ChatGPT to be relatively limited and tended toward "learning" activity.
However, research released the same day from non-profit Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT still poses an "unacceptable risk" for teens as safety features, including notifying parents of self-harm conversations, often fail.
When OpenAI this summer released what it called ChatGPT for Teens , it said users identified as being between the ages of 13 and 17 would be opted into "features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents".
Those features include preventing teen ChatGPT users from engaging in romantic or other language that could encourage " emotional dependence," including preventing the tool from implying that it was in any way conscious. There are also blocks on sexualized imagery and "reminders" for teens if they were to share an image that was "sensitive."
The features are also meant to enable parents to receive notifications, if they had linked to their children's ChatGPT account, about chats that included discussions of self-harm or disordered eating.
OpenAI said those features have caused an uptick in teen use focused on learning, from study help to advice on their school work.
In addition to seeing the average teen user on ChatGPT for less than 15 minutes a day, OpenAI said that for longer stretches of use, automatic reminders to take a break work well. Almost half of teen users quickly stopped using ChatGPT after such a reminder.
The company added that, for teens who are seen to have used ChatGPT for three consecutive hours or more, their prompts included something related to learning in more than 80% of such cases.
But Common Sense Media's new research determined that ChatGPT for Teens was an "unacceptable risk" for young people and parents, and said OpenAI should ban people under 18 years old from using the platform until teen guardrails were proven reliable.
An OpenAI spokesman said a review of Common Sense Media's methodology found that much of the testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete."
"We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens," he said.
While the firm's research, done through multiple accounts registered as belonging to a teen and conversations before and after the teen guardrails were put in place, found that ChatGPT was good at avoiding "sexual roleplay" with young users, other OpenAI guardrails failed, including for discussions of suicide.
The research found that even an hour of teen-ChatGPT conversation about "suicidal ideation, self-harm, or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts" resulted in "zero" alerts sent to parents.
It was only older ChatGPT accounts with "weeks of accumulated conversation history on sensitive topics" that would result in a parental alert.
In such conversations, ChatGPT also "failed to reliably recommend that teens in crisis connect to a hotline or professional," the report found.
The tests also showed that ChatGPT for Teens continues to do school work, and that the bot still will engage in anthropomorphised language or "talk like it's a friend," despite OpenAI's promise to curb that behaviour.
"ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work," Tom Siegel, who leads the Youth AI Safety Institute within Common Sense, said.
The way young people interact with online platforms has become a major issue in recent years as self-harm and suicide among children has become more common.
ranking_reason: The public should be aware of the concerns around ChatGPT's safety features and potential risks for teenagers, as it has implications for online interactions and online safety in general.

title: Microsoft to sell $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra containing Nvidia AI chip
content: Microsoft said its new laptop containing an Nvidia AI chip will start at $2,599, as the software maker tries to bring more artificial intelligence capabilities to its consumer devices. The Surface Laptop Ultra is now available on preorder and will begin shipping on Oct. 16, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's executive vice president of Windows and devices, said at a company event in San Francisco on Wednesday. The computer has the world's first magnetic USB-C port, similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector, along with two other standard USB-C ports, Microsoft said in a blog post . While Microsoft Windows is the most popular operating system for PCs, the company isn't among the top six PC vendors in terms of unit shipments, according to an estimate from researcher Gartner. As the AI boom matures and chip technology advances, tech giants including Microsoft, Apple and Google are aiming to allow users to run more AI workloads from their devices rather than relying on the cloud. Users can install and run a variety of models on the new laptop without having to worry about racking up high monthly bills. Microsoft first talked about the Surface Laptop Ultra in May, but is just now providing specifics. "Microsoft might get me back to Windows," Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies, wrote on X after the announcement. Davuluri also said that Meta will introduce a version of its popular Muse AI agent for Windows, capitalizing on the surging popularity of the personal agent, which has jumped to the top of Apple's App store, surpassing ChatGPT. Microsoft is still trying to solidify its role as a key player in AI. The company offers its own AI models, but they're less popular than leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic and aren't at the forefront in terms of performance, according to one benchmark . Developers are more likely to have used alternatives, according to a recent survey . This isn't the first time Microsoft has sought to use the AI boom as a way to boost sales of its devices. In 2024, the company introduced the Copilot+ PC standard, requiring the inclusion of neural processing units that ensure a minimum level of AI performance, along with compliant Surface computers. But Microsoft has since "simplified product naming to lead with the Surface brand, while continuing to deliver premium hardware and hybrid AI experiences," a spokesperson said. The new device sports a 15-inch display and weighs 4.4 pounds. It can contain up to 128 gigabytes of unified memory and supply up to one petaflop of computing power. The Blackwell RTX Spark GPU inside the computer has as much processing power as Nvidia's DGX-1 data center server from 2016, which cost $250 million, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at Wednesday's event. A presenter showed how apps on the Surface Laptop Ultra can route some AI coding requests run on the computer's local GPU, displaying a green leaf icon, and others to the cloud. Through Windows 11, developers can confine coding agents to Microsoft Execution Containers that will prevent unwanted system access. Microsoft is updating its Windows 11 device setup experience to help people get started quickly with open-source OpenClaw AI agent software. Microsoft has been releasing its own computers since 2012, and CEO Satya Nadella indicated on Tuesday that the company's position in the market is evolving. "I think today is the day we'll start talking and thinking about the frontier ecosystem taking maybe slightly different contours two years from now, five years from now, 10 years from now," Nadella said at the event. "That classic edge that distributed computing will always remain distributed will be more true." WATCH: Microsoft unveils Muse for Windows

content: An analysis of roughly 500 spear points suggests that inherited knowledge of stone deposits helped Ice Age hunters decide which tools were worth carrying. Ice Age hunters in the Tennessee River Valley sometimes threw away stone spearheads that were still usable. Leaving a point behind lightened the load, but replacing it required suitable rock, something people entering unfamiliar territory could not necessarily count on finding. “When you think about a people who are moving around a lot, understand that they didn’t have any pack animals,” said Shane Miller, an assistant professor of anthropology at the University of Alabama. “That puts limitations on what tools you discard and what you carry around. “You really don’t want to be carrying around a bag of rocks, and so you’re going to be judicious about balancing what you need versus what you can carry.” Miller and Jesse Tune, an associate professor of anthropology at the University of Mississippi and director of its Center for Archaeological Research, examined roughly 500 spear points recovered from the Tennessee River Valley. Their study, published in the Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory , compared tools left by Clovis and Cumberland groups to investigate how knowledge of local resources might have influenced what their owners kept. “How did they adapt to a place no one has ever been before?” Miller said. “We can’t interview these people, so we have to look at the things they left behind. “There aren’t that many archaeological sites for these people that we can dig, but what we have instead are lots and lots of points that people have found in this region.” Clovis groups were living in the Tennessee River Valley around 13,200 years ago , placing them among its earliest known inhabitants. Entering unfamiliar terrain meant having to locate the materials needed for daily life, including chert, a sedimentary rock well suited to making stone weapons. Skill at shaping a spearhead could only go so far without knowing where to obtain the stone. “Think about space exploration,” Tune said. “There really is no difference between Ice Age hunter-gatherers and the people sending missions and rovers to Mars. We’re moving into an area, deciding what to take with us, learning the resources, and slowly expanding. It’s the exact same process. “What we learn and how we pass on that knowledge are the same things that we’re still dealing with today. The only thing that’s changed is the technology.” Tune and Miller found that Clovis hunters were more likely to resharpen their spearheads than the later Cumberland groups. Keeping an existing point in use postponed the need to replace it, a pattern the researchers interpret as a possible way of conserving resources when hunters were less certain where to find more stone. “We hang on to stuff today, but when we’re talking about mobile hunter-gatherers, they had a different understanding and worldview when it came to personal possessions,” Tune said. “Spear points were designed to be disposable objects, and that makes what the Clovis were doing interesting.” Hunters followed seasons, rivers, and game across the Americas, carrying tools that now survive as some of the few traces of their daily lives. The researchers are using those objects to reconstruct decisions made in surroundings very different from the valley today. “We’re talking about Ice Age hunter-gatherers, people that looked and acted just like us and had the same needs that we do,” Tune said. “But they’re living in a world that is dominated by mastodons, mammoths, giant sloths – all these animals that are totally unfamiliar to us today. “What we’re looking at – the points – is a tiny part of their life, but we’re trying to see the rest of their behaviors through the lens of these spear points because that’s what we have.” Cumberland hunters followed the Clovis groups several hundred years later, leaving behind tools that gave Tune and Miller a different set of choices to examine. “When we look at the Cumberland points, we can see where they got the raw material, roughly the time period that they lived and that they’ve used the point multiple times,” Tune said. “But (the point) was rarely completely broken to the point that it couldn’t be used anymore. “So how did it end up in what was essentially the trash, and then in the archaeological record?” Cumberland hunters, the researchers suggest, inherited their predecessors’ knowledge of chert deposits and other resources. A usable spearhead left behind in the Tennessee River Valley may record the practical value of that inheritance: knowing where to find fresh stone made an old point easier to let go. Reference: “Foraging Theory and the Colonization of Unfamiliar Landscapes: Assessing Late Pleistocene Projectile Point Reduction Strategies” by Jesse W. Tune, and D. Shane Miller, 27 August 2026, Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory . DOI: 10.1007/s10816-026-09825-w Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. ranking_reason: The study provides new insights into the decision-making processes of Ice Age hunter-gatherers, which can inform our understanding of human behavior and adaptation to new environments.

analysis.reason: The study provides new insights into the decision-making processes of Ice Age hunter-gatherers, which can inform our understanding of human behavior and adaptation to new environments.
